t: International Business Got More Concrete When I Picked a Product
d: What a small desk-research exercise on Tunisian olive oil and Singapore taught me about market-entry questions.
x:
I used to think of international business as a broad thing: companies in different countries, distributors, prices, rules, and people trying to sell across borders. That list is true, but it is so broad that it is hard to learn much from it.

For a small exercise, I worked with a specific product market pair: Tunisian olive oil and Singapore. I used an AI assistant to help me find public data and organise the questions. I wanted to see what could be learned before talking to an importer or pretending to make a business recommendation.

The first useful number was not a margin or a forecast. Singapore imported about 2.80 million kilograms of olive oil in 2024, worth US$25.50 million, according to  WITS' UN Comtrade data  https://wits.worldbank.org/trade/comtrade/en/country/SGP/year/2024/tradeflow/Imports/partner/ALL/product/1509 . Spain supplied about 1.70 million kilograms and Italy about 885,000. Tunisia's recorded quantity was only 130 kilograms.

That changed the question I was asking. A large market does not automatically make an opening for every exporter. Those figures tell me the category already has suppliers with strong positions; they do not tell me whether a retailer would give a Tunisian brand shelf space, what a bottle would cost after shipping, or whether customers would pay enough to support the business.

The import rules made the gap between an interesting idea and a real plan even clearer. The  Singapore Food Agency's guidance  https://www.sfa.gov.sg/food import export/commercial imports/what you need to know for import of food  says that importing processed food for commercial sale involves registration and the relevant permits. Someone would need to confirm the exact paperwork for the proposed product, not just put "export to Singapore" in a spreadsheet.

This was desk research, with AI help, not field research. I haven't contacted buyers or exporters and I don't have a shipping quote. But I now have better questions than "Is Singapore a good market?" I would want to know which olive oil segment a Tunisian producer could credibly serve, how store prices compare by size and origin, what an importer would require, and what the landed cost looks like using actual quotes.

I am starting to understand international business as the work of narrowing a broad opportunity into a specific decision with costs, rules, competitors and evidence. The full case, including the data table and source links, is in  the market entry study  /projects/market entry hypothetical product/ .

d: A distinction that matters when the goal is an agreement rather than a change of mind.
x:
I keep coming back to a basic difference: changing someone's mind is not the same job as agreeing what to do next.

Imagine a contractor and a client arguing over a Friday deadline. The client keeps saying the date was promised; the contractor keeps explaining why the remaining work needs another day. They are trying to win different versions of the same argument. But the decision in front of them might be narrower: what can be delivered on Friday, what moves to Monday, and whether the changed schedule affects the price.

That example is hypothetical, but it makes the distinction easier to see. Persuasion tries to change a belief or preference. Negotiation tries to settle terms when people have different priorities. Sometimes you need both. Sometimes you can agree on a workable arrangement while still disagreeing about who was right.

One part I find easy to overlook is that a demand may hide a constraint. A deadline might stand in for another commitment. A price may reflect a budget limit rather than a judgement about quality. Those are possible explanations, not facts about the other person. Asking is safer than assuming you know what they mean.

The practical question is what can actually change. Maybe the deadline cannot move, but the scope can. Maybe the price is fixed but support, timing, or payment terms are not. If nothing can change, then the honest question is whether there is any agreement available at all.

I have not documented a real negotiation using a formal method, so I won't claim this is a tested framework. For me, the distinction is useful as a way to read a disagreement: are we trying to change the other person's view, or do we need to make a decision together? I don't need to turn every disagreement into an argument to win.

t: Tunisian Olive Oil in Singapore: A First-Pass Market Study
d: A desk-research exercise using trade data and Singapore's official import guidance to find out what needs checking before anyone recommends market entry.
x:
The question

Could a Tunisian olive oil producer find a place in Singapore? I chose a real product and a real destination so I could work with evidence instead of a country level checklist. This is a first pass desk study, not a recommendation to export.

I used an AI assistant to help locate and organise public sources. The source links are included so the figures can be checked directly. I have not interviewed Singaporean buyers, contacted an importer, audited supermarket shelves, or obtained shipping quotes.

   What the numbers say

The World Bank's WITS page, using UN Comtrade data, reports Singapore's 2024 imports of olive oil under HS 1509 at 2,795,220 kg worth US$25.50 million. The figures below are reported values unless marked as a calculation.

| Item | Finding | How to read it |
|     |     |     |
| Singapore, total imports in 2024 | 2,795,220 kg; US$25.50 million | A real import market exists, but this total includes different olive oil products and does not tell me what any one segment will pay. |
| Spain | 1,704,470 kg; US$15.83 million | About 61.0% of reported import volume. |
| Italy | 884,710 kg; US$7.44 million | About 31.6% of reported import volume. |
| Spain and Italy together | About 92.6% of volume | Calculated from the reported quantities. This suggests a market with established suppliers, not an easy opening. |
| Tunisia | 130 kg; about US$1,800 | A very small recorded flow in this dataset, around 0.0046% of total volume. It does not prove that Tunisian oil could not sell there. |
| Average import value | About US$9.12 per kg overall | Calculation: total declared value divided by total quantity. This is not a retail price or a supplier quote. |
| Tunisia's recorded unit value | About US$13.85 per kg | Calculation from only 130 kg. The quantity is too small to use as a sensible pricing benchmark. |

Source:  WITS / UN Comtrade, Singapore olive oil imports in 2024  https://wits.worldbank.org/trade/comtrade/en/country/SGP/year/2024/tradeflow/Imports/partner/ALL/product/1509 . Figures and percentages are rounded. The page uses HS 1509, so the figures should not be treated as an extra virgin only market estimate.

   Regulatory facts to check early

Singapore's Food Agency says businesses importing processed food for commercial sale must be registered with SFA and must obtain the relevant import permit through TradeNet. Importers also need to meet Singapore's food rules. Before making a shipment, the exact product category, code, labelling and supporting documents should be confirmed for the oil and packaging in question.

Source:  Singapore Food Agency, import of food for commercial sale  https://www.sfa.gov.sg/food import export/commercial imports/what you need to know for import of food .

Singapore's IRAS explains that import GST is 9% of the applicable taxable value, which includes the cost, insurance and freight value and any customs duties payable. A real landed cost model would need a freight quote, the correct customs classification, importer charges and advice on how GST applies to the business. The percentage alone is not the total cost of entry.

Source:  IRAS, importing goods  https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/goods services tax %28gst%29/claiming gst %28input tax%29/importing of goods .

   Facts, estimates and unanswered questions

| Type | Current note | Next check |
|     |     |     |
| Fact | Singapore imported about 2.80 million kg of HS 1509 olive oil in 2024. | Confirm the product segments and check whether a newer full year data set is available. |
| Fact | Spain and Italy account for most of the reported volume. | Compare brands, origins, pack sizes and shelf prices in Singapore stores. |
| Fact | Tunisia's recorded quantity in the data is only 130 kg. | Check whether this was a one off consignment, a reporting quirk, or a broader pattern across years. |

d: A multi-stage AI research agent for comparing arguments about metaphysics and religion, including a failure I found in its own reasoning pipeline.
x:
What I built

I made an AI assisted research program to investigate questions about ultimate reality, starting with cosmology and necessary existence and eventually reaching questions about consciousness, morality, and religion. The point was to keep the steps between a premise and a conclusion visible instead of asking one model for a final answer.

The current source config sets the model name to  gemini flash latest  and uses Google's Gemini API. I built around the free tier through Google AI Studio because I wanted the project to cost nothing to run. Provider limits and model names can change, so the repository configuration is the source of truth for the current default.

 Open the code on GitHub  https://github.com/TheSunNeverRose/Ultimate Reality Researcher .

   How a cycle is meant to work

The repo defines 12 stages, from existence and cosmology through metaphysics, mind, morality, revelation, and comparative religion. Each cycle chooses a question for the current stage, gathers sources, has opposing arguments examined, updates stored state, and selects what to investigate next.

   text
Research question and stage
            |
            v
Propositions and dependencies  P1 P8 
            |
      +     +      +
      |            |
      v            v
Argument builder  Critical researcher
      |            |
      +     +      +
            v
     Four round debate
            |
            v
   Adjudication / synthesis
            |
            v
 Evidence, verdict and confidence
            |
            v
 SQLite memory    next question / report
   

The current implementation uses two opposing research agents and an adjudicator. The code separates their roles, records source information, stores debate data in SQLite, and can generate Markdown reports. These pieces are visible in   debate.py   https://github.com/TheSunNeverRose/Ultimate Reality Researcher/blob/main/debate.py L280 L296 ,   researcher.py   https://github.com/TheSunNeverRose/Ultimate Reality Researcher/blob/main/researcher.py L672 L699 , and   config.py   https://github.com/TheSunNeverRose/Ultimate Reality Researcher/blob/main/config.py L21 L25 .

There is also an offline fallback. If the model call fails or its response cannot be parsed into the expected structure, the program can use preset fallback content and keep going. Each cycle records an  is offline fallback  flag. That is useful for resilience, but it matters when judging a result: a cycle completing does not by itself prove that Gemini supplied fresh analysis.

   A run pattern that made me suspicious

In an earlier run sequence, around cycles 7 to 25, the system kept returning to the Borde Guth Vilenkin theorem and the second law of thermodynamics when arguing for a finite cosmic past. The conclusion was labelled   PROBABLY   in the run I was tracking. This is a summary from my notes, not a verbatim transcript, and it refers to that earlier run rather than a guaranteed result from the current version.

The problem was not that those arguments are irrelevant. It was that seeing the same arguments again did not show that the investigation had improved. I could not point to a clear new source, a counterargument that had been resolved, or a change in the premises that explained why a later cycle deserved more confidence than an earlier one.

The BGV theorem concerns past incompleteness under its expansion condition. That is not automatically the same as proving that absolutely all reality began to exist, and it does not establish that a cause beyond the universe must be personal. The thermodynamic argument also depends on the cosmological and entropy model being assumed. Those steps need their own arguments, not just a citation to the theorem.

The paper is available here:  Borde, Guth and Vilenkin,  Inflationary Spacetimes Are Incomplete in Past Directions   2003   https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.90.151301 .
